picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: Trains 4+ times a week and already buys supplements and recovery products, so replenishment volume is high. Price sensitivity is low-medium, so the pitch is not 'cheap' but 'same formula, more of it'.
lean_into: clinically used doses that actually perform
stock up without changing your stack
picks.ad_angle: Same formulations the expensive brands use — keep your performance, double your supply.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Tracks supplements and workouts and responds to science-backed claims and ingredient transparency, which fits the brand's 'same formulations' claim. Price sensitivity is low, so lead with label scrutiny rather than discounts.
picks.ad_angle: Compare the labels: identical ingredients to the premium tubs — you're paying for marketing, not efficacy.

picks.name: The Value-Conscious Shopper
picks.why_plausible: High price sensitivity and responds to discount-forward, clear value props and bundle offers, which is exactly this brand's whole positioning. Supplements are a recurring replenishment buy where cost adds up.
lean_into: half the cost of the big brands
picks.ad_angle: Half the price per serving — do the math on your monthly supplement bill.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Medium price sensitivity, buys in bulk and replenishes household staples; a parent squeezing in gym time wants protein that doesn't blow the family budget. Disinterested in luxury positioning, which this brand never uses.
picks.ad_angle: Protein that fits the family budget — bulk restock for the parent who still makes it to the gym.

plan.summary: No direct supplement competitors block the plan, so it anchors on Movewell's fitness-engaged apparel audience with fitness-services, supplement and functional-beverage tests, while the long tail of apparel, pet and home publishers drops out as off-category.

recommended.name: Movewell
recommended.adjustment_reason: Notes say 'Fitness-engaged shoppers', the single closest behavioral match to gym-goers buying supplements, and 22M impressions is the largest reach among non-excluded publishers — the values score (21) understates fit because it penalizes a price-led brand rather than a category mismatch.
recommended.rationale: Movewell's 'Fitness-engaged shoppers' are the people who actually buy pre-workout and protein, and at $78 typical order a $40 supplement offer reads as an easy add-on. Highest usable reach in the plan at 22M monthly impressions.
recommended.risk: 82% female and mid-high income; creatine/pre-workout creative skewed to male lifters or leaning hard on 'half the cost' may not land with this activewear buyer.

test.name: Studiogrid
test.rationale: Studiogrid books fitness classes and personal training, so buyers are mid-workout-routine and the $42 typical spend sits right at the $40 supplement price. Natural moment to pitch replenishable protein or creatine.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

test.risk: A high-income, 28-50, spa-and-yoga audience skews away from price-led lifting supplements; the 'half the cost' hook is the weakest part of the pitch here.

test.name: Daily Form
test.rationale: Closest category match in the catalog — this audience already buys vitamins and supplements at a near-identical $38 order — but that overlap is exactly why it is capped at test spend.

evidence.quote: Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims

test.risk: Notes flag an audience 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims', and the brief's 'Same formulations as the expensive brands' is a bare assertion; without label proof this placement can backfire. Also 89% female versus a lifter-coded product.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.rationale: Pantrygood shoppers buy replenishable consumables and respond to 'clean-ingredient' and wellness claims, which is adjacent to protein but not the same intent as gym supplementation.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: Notes describe 'Values-driven shoppers' at high income — a brand that competes on price rather than sourcing or sustainability has little to say to them.

test.name: Cloudfoot
test.rationale: Activewear footwear gives a plausible fitness read, but at $118 a typical order this is a comfort-and-sustainability buyer, not a price-comparing lifter.
test.risk: 'Tech-adjacent urban professionals' at 5.8M impressions means thin volume and an audience unmoved by a budget pitch.

bid_strategy.rationale: $40 first order × 0.30 = $12.00 target CPA: one-time purchase, so the first order has to pay back the acquisition. The max CPA allows headroom while the campaign learns over 14 days.

frequency_cap.rationale: Offers appear once, right after checkout; repeating them reads as spam.

experiment.graduate_rule: After 14 days, move a test publisher to core if its CPA is at or below target; cut any placement above max CPA.
experiment.notes: Creatives rotate evenly until each has enough conversions to compare.
